title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
description: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.L
body: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery."The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier.""I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off."I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external. A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics"."We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

schema.headline: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis

title: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
description: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated
body: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.All were told they could never serve in the police again.The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.The case was heard by a panel of five judges.The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

schema.headline: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer

title: Mamdani reveals plan for closure of New York's Rikers Island jail
description: New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of
body: New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.  Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population. Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates. Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.  It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said. The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein. It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union. "[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges." Kaplan disagreed."It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said. The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays. Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility. In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it. New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan. Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029,  two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032. The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours. Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process. He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues. Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.  The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

schema.headline: Mamdani reveals plan for closure of New York's Rikers Island jail

title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
description: Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they ar
body: Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal."It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas. "We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said. For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed. The world is entering a period called "overshoot". Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat. The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations. Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources. Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas, external. The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - that figure has now been removed."We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations."I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected", said one observer.

schema.headline: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock

title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah to meet India PM Modi on first bilateral visit
description: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's ne
body: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset."The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC."They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further."India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas."I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough."Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says  Dixit.Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

schema.headline: Nepal PM Balendra Shah to meet India PM Modi on first bilateral visit

title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
description: A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isi
body: A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

schema.headline: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
description: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged marke
body: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth."As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said."Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.But tech stocks more broadly also fell.Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

schema.headline: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide

title: Indian man gets 19-plus years in assassination plot of Sikh leader
description: A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.Nikh
body: A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs. Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court."He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government. The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event"."It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at  demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun said the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism."I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

schema.headline: Indian man gets 19-plus years in assassination plot of Sikh leader

title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "frien
body: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said. Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war"."They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer"."I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure". The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare"."This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

schema.headline: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

title: South Africa's local elections: ANC fights to keep control of cities after election setback
description: While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.Bu
body: While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.This is what voters want.The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg."I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

schema.headline: South Africa's local elections: ANC fights to keep control of cities after election setback

title: They were fined $811m for conning migrants - the scams didn't stop
description: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being
body: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.Their firm, Libre By Nexus,  which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable. In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company."I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.  "I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund.  A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company. Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation."Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed."But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss"."The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention.  "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

schema.headline: They were fined $811m for conning migrants - the scams didn't stop

title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis
description: Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local governm
body: Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials sayByOrla GuerinSenior international correspondentReporting fromIstanbulIn the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie."When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the cityOn streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers."Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz."It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors."I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decadeWar is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor saysIf the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards."Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us."The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."We have not been able to independently verify these figures.He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance."Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.How long can the city hold out, I ask."Until the population perishes," he replies.Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindlingMany in Taiz are resisting.They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.He tells us this fight is different to 2015."This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union."They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent monthsBut it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest."Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.But could they fight their way in?Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does."Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away."I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community."Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

schema.headline: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis

title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
description: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so."We're
body: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so."We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in."We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia."Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear."I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November."You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said."We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres. Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".Google has been contacted for comment.

schema.headline: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas

title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
description: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "init
body: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia". Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly". In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services."This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September. Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said. He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

schema.headline: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper

title: Palisades fire: Man guilty of starting one of California's deadliest blazes
description: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days l
body: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze."We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California. Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured"."So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

schema.headline: Palisades fire: Man guilty of starting one of California's deadliest blazes
